plain: Runway is a set of AI video tools that goes beyond generating shots: besides creating video from text or an image, it edits video you already have. It can erase an object from a scene and fill in the gap, separate a person from the background without a green screen, extend a shot, change the style of an entire video, or generate the missing piece. It's the tool for someone who already has footage and needs to fix or extend it, more than for someone starting from scratch.

account.free: There's a free plan with a handful of one-time-use credits, a watermark, and limited resolution: good for checking if it's for you, not for real work. Paid plans started around $15 a month as of August 2026, and rise quite a bit for plans meant for daily production. Credits are consumed per second of generated video and per tool, so the same plan can cover very little or quite a lot depending on what you do. Check runwayml.com and, as always, verify commercial use and watermark rules before invoicing anything.
steps: Go to runwayml.com and sign up
With Google. You'll find a dashboard with tools separated by what they do, not a single text box: that's the difference from the other tools.

Generate (text or image to video), edit (erase objects, separate from background, extend), and transform (change the style of an existing video). Once you know which one you're in, the tool stops feeling like a maze.
Start by editing something of your own
Upload a short video you shot with your phone and try erasing an object from the scene. It's where Runway shines and where you'll quickly see what it's good for.
Each one costs differently and is charged per second generated. Before a session, check how much what you're about to do will cost: four seconds of generation can cost the same as five edits.
Decide the framing and movement with short, cheap generations, and only once it's decided, generate the final version in high quality.
Same as with all these tools: check it before accepting a client job, not after delivering it.
account.warning: Same as with the rest of the video tools: don't generate or modify video with identifiable people without their permission, and even less so with well-known faces. And be careful what you upload: if the footage is a client's, check your contract first for what it says about processing it through third-party services.

first: Upload a short video of your own, under ten seconds, shot with your phone.
Try erasing an object from the scene with the erase tool: it's the one that best demonstrates what this is for.
Try separating a person from the background without a green screen and giving them a different background. You'll see where it fails: hair and edges.
Generate a short shot from one of your images and compare it to the original video: you'll understand what it adds and what it doesn't.
Note how many credits each thing cost you. It's the information you need to plan any job.
shortcuts: Starting from a photo and putting it in motion. Same as the others: much more predictable than starting from text alone.
You point at something in the video and it's removed, filling the gap with what should be behind it. It's one of the best things it does.
Cuts out the person or object without needing a green screen. Works very well except for hair and fast-moving edges.
Continues a video that turned out too short. Useful when your edit is two seconds short and you can't reshoot.
Applies a different look to an existing video. Spectacular in a demo and hard to control in real work.
During generation you can indicate movement: zoom in, zoom out, pan. Less guided than in Higgsfield but it's there.
Test in low, deliver in high. Deciding the framing at maximum quality is throwing credits away.
Everything generated, with its settings. It's your archive and your way of repeating what worked.
daily: Be clear on which family you're in: generate, edit, or transform. Most of the frustration with Runway comes from using the generate tool for something that's solved by editing.
Upload your own footage whenever you can. Runway shines fixing and extending what already exists, more than inventing from scratch.
Test in low resolution and deliver in high. It's the habit that saves the most credits across the whole tool.
Think in short shots. Same as the rest: five to ten seconds, and the video is assembled afterward.
Check edges and hair when separating from the background. That's where it fails, and where the eye goes immediately.
Calculate credits before accepting a job. They're charged per second generated and per tool: the same plan can cover very little or quite a lot depending on what you do.

templates.name: The decision sheet: generate, edit, or transform
templates.what: The mistake that costs the most time and credits in Runway is using the wrong tool for your problem. This sheet reads in a minute and decides for you, based on what you already have shot.
templates.how: 1) Always start with the first question: what material do I have. 2) Follow the branch. 3) Only once you know the tool, write the brief. 4) Test in low resolution. 5) Note the real cost in credits for next time.
fill: Almost always the answer is edit, not regenerate
Extending the shot usually turns out better and cheaper than generating a new one
Generate from an image before generating from plain text
templates.code:
┌─ WHAT DO I ALREADY HAVE? ────────────────────────────────
│
├─ I have the video and something's in the way (a person,
│  a sign, an object)
│     → ERASE OBJECT. Don't regenerate the whole shot.
│
├─ I have the video and want to change the background
│     → SEPARATE FROM BACKGROUND. Check hair and edges after.
│
├─ I have the video but it comes up short in the edit
│     → EXTEND SHOT. Cheaper and more consistent than
│       generating a new one that won't match.
│
├─ I have a photo and want motion
│     → IMAGE TO VIDEO. 5 to 10 second shot.
│
├─ I have the video and want a different overall look
│     → TRANSFORM STYLE. Warning: hard to control,
│       set aside credits for several attempts.
│
└─ I have nothing
      → First get or generate a good IMAGE.
        Then, image to video. Direct text to video
        is the option with the most rejects.

─── BEFORE GENERATING AT FINAL QUALITY ────────────────────
[ ] Framing and movement decided at low resolution
[ ] Credit cost calculated
[ ] Watermark and commercial use checked
[ ] No one identifiable without permission

errors: Erasing an object leaves a smudge or a flicker where it was

The fill didn't find enough information about what was behind it. Try marking an area a bit wider than the object, and if the camera was moving a lot, do it in shorter chunks. If the object was covering something complex (a face, text), sometimes there's no fix and you have to reframe.
When separating from the background, hair and edges come out messy

It's a known limitation of these tools. It helps if the original has good contrast between subject and background and no very fast motion. If the result will be shown large, review frame by frame the moments of most movement before calling it good.
I burned through my credits in two generations

They're charged per second generated and per tool, and high-quality video generation is the most expensive of all. The rule is non-negotiable: decide at low resolution, generate at high quality once. And calculate the cost before accepting the job.
The generated video has nothing to do with what I asked for

Almost always it's text-to-video with a description of feelings instead of a description of what's seen. Start from an image if you can, and describe subject, setting, light, and movement instead of adjectives.
The extended shot doesn't match the original
You asked for too many seconds at once: the more it extends, the further it drifts. Ask for less time, and if you need a lot, do it in two passes checking in between.
Free plan. It's not removed by cropping. It's solved with the paid plan, and it's checked before generating the final version, not after showing it to the client.

prompts.name: Decide which Runway tool solves my problem
prompts.prompt: I have a problem with a video and I don't know if it's solved by generating something new, editing what I have, or transforming it. Help me decide before I spend credits. One: ask me what footage I already have shot, how long it is, what needs removing, what's missing, and where the final video is for. Two: tell me which specific Runway tool solves my case and why that one and not another, keeping in mind that editing is usually cheaper and more consistent than regenerating. Three: tell me which parts of my problem this tool does NOT solve, and what does solve them, even if it's outside Runway or means reshooting. Four: give me the order of work, starting with the part most likely to fail, so I find out early if the plan doesn't work. Five: give me a credit estimate, telling me how many attempts is reasonable to budget per step. Six: tell me what I should check in the result of each step before moving to the next, because chaining errors here gets expensive. My footage is: [DESCRIBE IT] and what I need to achieve is: [DESCRIBE IT].

words: Credit
The currency. Consumed per second generated and varies by tool. High-quality generation is the most expensive.
Image to video
Starting from a photo and putting it in motion. The most predictable option.
Inpainting / erase object
Removing something from the scene and filling the gap with what should be behind it.
Separate from background
Cutting out the subject without needing a green screen. Fails on hair and fast edges.
Extend
Continuing a shot that came up short. Better to ask for a small amount of time each time.
Transform style
Applying a different look to an existing video. Eye-catching and hard to control.
Shot
A continuous chunk of video, five to ten seconds. The unit of work.
Test resolution
Generating at low quality to decide. It's the habit that saves the most credits.
Watermark
The free plan's mark. Removed with the paid plan, not by editing.
Commercial use
Whether your plan lets you use what's generated in a job you're paid for.
matters: Telling generate apart from edit. Most real video problems are solved by editing what you already have, which is cheaper, faster, and more consistent than generating from scratch.
Testing in low resolution and delivering in high. It's the rule that separates burning through the month's plan in one afternoon from making it last.
Checking hair and edges when separating from the background. It always fails there, and it's where the eye goes immediately.
Calculating credits before accepting a job. Here cost depends so much on the tool that the same plan can cover very little or quite a lot.
ignore: Changing the style of an entire video while you're still learning. It's the flashiest thing in a demo and the hardest to control in real work with a deadline.
Pure text to video. With your own footage or a starting image, results are much better with far fewer rejects.
The new features that come out every month. Learn erase object, separate from background, and image to video well: with those three you solve almost everything you'll be asked to do.
